tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

input.prompt:
Research empirical academic and industry studies (2025 to October 2026) on the STRUCTURAL and ARCHITECTURAL quality of LLM/agent-generated code.

Context: the findings feed feature ideas for "archy", an open-source Python architecture-analysis CLI + MCP server for coding agents. It already ships: import graph, layer rules (check), import-linter contracts, cycles, DSM, impact/affected, co-change coupling from git, hotspots (complexity x churn), duplicates (identical function clusters), derived "conventions" headers, composite score, snapshot/diff/trend, simulate (predict structural consequence of an edit), what-to-refactor-next, brief (one screen for an agent before a task). So we want evidence of WHICH architectural failure modes agent code actually exhibits, measured, so we can tell which detectors would catch real problems.

Key questions:
- What do measured studies say about LLM/agent code and coupling, cohesion, modularity, layering violations, dependency cycles, architecture erosion/drift, duplication/copy-paste (e.g. GitClear 2025 follow-ups), dead code, code churn, technical debt, maintainability?
- Studies of agentic PRs in the wild (e.g. AIDev dataset, Claude Code / Codex / Copilot agent PRs on GitHub): what structural problems reviewers reject them for? Acceptance rates and reasons.
- Studies on "vibe coding" and long-horizon degradation of codebases maintained by agents (e.g. SWE-bench-style multi-step evolution benchmarks, maintainability benchmarks, "slop" accumulation).
- Any study that measured architecture-conformance checks, static analysis, or structural feedback improving agent output (or failing to). Report nulls as carefully as positives.
- Concrete numbers, sample sizes, venues, dates, and links.

Suggested sources: arXiv (cs.SE), ICSE/FSE/ASE/MSR 2025-2026 proceedings, GitClear, METR, Google/DORA reports, CodeScene research, Sonar reports, industry engineering blogs with data.

Constraints: prioritize 2025-2026 publications; mark older ones as background. Distinguish measured findings from opinion. Note any skepticism or failed replications. Be honest about weak evidence.

input.prompt:
Research 2025 to October 2026 papers and evidence on giving coding agents repository-level STRUCTURAL context (code graphs, dependency info, architecture rules, repo maps) and whether it measurably helps.

Context: findings feed feature ideas for "archy", an open-source Python architecture-analysis CLI + MCP server for coding agents (import graph, layer rules, cycles, DSM, impact, co-change coupling, hotspots, duplicates, derived conventions headers, score, simulate, brief). IMPORTANT prior result: archy measured six interventions that push structural facts at agents (MCP tools, headers in source files, briefs, etc.) and none produced a positive effect on agent outcomes; two cost MORE tokens than control. So we especially need evidence about WHEN structural context helps and when it does not, and what the measured effect sizes are.

Key questions:
- Repo-level code graph papers and their measured gains: RepoGraph, CodexGraph, LocAgent, CodeRAG, OrcaLoca, KGCompass, Agentless, SWE-agent ACI work, Moatless, AutoCodeRover, and 2026 successors. What tasks (localization vs. repair vs. generation) benefit?
- Studies on AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / context files effectiveness (e.g. 2025-2026 papers evaluating context files, which reportedly found little or negative effect). Studies on MCP tool use by agents, tool overload, tool selection.
- Benchmarks measuring architecture/design quality or maintainability of agent output, not only test-passing: e.g. SWE-bench variants, refactoring benchmarks, "design" or "architecture" benchmarks, multi-step codebase evolution benchmarks, code-review benchmarks.
- Evidence on feedback-loop placement: does static/structural feedback AFTER an edit (lint-in-the-loop, verification, CI-style gates) help more than context BEFORE? Any measured numbers.
- Concrete effect sizes, models used, venues, dates, links.

Suggested sources: arXiv cs.SE/cs.AI, ICSE/FSE/ASE/NeurIPS/ICLR 2025-2026, SWE-bench leaderboard writeups, Anthropic/OpenAI/Google engineering posts on context engineering.

Constraints: 2025-2026 focus; mark older as background. Report negative and null results prominently. Distinguish measured from claimed.

---
name: feedback_vet_proposals_anti_theater
description: "vet archy feature proposals against the anti-theater test + OECD axis gate BEFORE filing tickets, especially when motivated by an external paper"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: cead1646-5733-444f-b9b4-7d5429ba3aa3
---

When proposing archy features (tickets, specs, design docs), run them through the
project's own metric-vetting gates BEFORE filing, not after. This applies especially
when the motivation is an external paper or authority (e.g. the 2000 ADL classification
paper), because "an authoritative source says X matters" is precisely the reasoning
those gates exist to distrust.

The two gates, both already documented in-repo:
- **Anti-theater test** (maintainer's PR #142/#143 principle, quoted throughout
  `docs/research/AGENT_CAUSAL_REASONING_SYNTHESIS.md`): *what does an agent or human do
  differently because of this?* A different action, not a different dashboard. A new
  number/axis/synthesis that changes no user action is the "vanity thermometer."
- **OECD four-condition gate** (`docs/research/AXIS_REVIEW.md`), required if a signal
  would reach the score: independence, directionality, actionability, discriminant
  validity. This is what rejected `calls_per_edge` and type-hint coverage as axes.

Also weigh against the maintainer's recorded 2026-05-26 prioritization: the
highest-leverage next move is a **usage signal** (does anyone call archy inside an
agent loop?), not more capability. "More capability" proposals sit below that line
until usage evidence exists.

**Why:** on 2026-07-12 I proposed, filed (#270 typed connectors, #271 conformance),
and merged a spec justified purely by ADL-paper fit, skipping both gates. The user
caught it. The features mostly held up on re-analysis, but the process gap (external
authority -> file -> merge, with no gate) was the real miss.

**How to apply:** before writing a proposal ticket, state explicitly what action an
agent/human takes differently because of the feature; if the answer is "reads a nicer
number," stop or re-scope to the consumer. For any score-reaching signal, run the four
OECD conditions. Prefer tools/packaging a user calls and acts on over new numbers.
Relates to [[feedback_use_deepwork_review]] and [[project_archy_next_up]].

- Release: bump `pyproject.toml`, `src/archy/__init__.py`, `server.json` (x2),

  after merge create the GitHub release via `gh api` (tag `vX.Y.Z`, target main),

  `docs/MCP_DIRECTORIES.md` is a dated record and was left at 0.46.2.

  ([[verify-tests-by-mutation]]), clear `__pycache__` between mutants.
- Pre-existing review findings get filed, not folded in; grep existing issues
  (state=all) for duplicates first. Review via DeepWork ([[use-deepwork-review]]);
  a reviewer may call `mark_review_as_passed` and then report a FAIL, so trust the
  write-up, not the recorded verdict.
- Always `gh api` REST ([[github-rest-not-graphql]]).
- `skills/archy/SKILL.md` has a byte-identical copy at
  `plugins/claude/skills/archy/SKILL.md`; `cp` it, `tests/test_plugin.py` gates.
- CI gates include `archy conventions . --emit-headers --check`; regenerate with
  `--write`, never hand-edit a block.
- `bench/walkthrough.py` is a real gate: it caught a translation change that
  silently altered how bare layer patterns behave.
- Wiring a payload field: CLI text, CLI JSON, MCP return model, and assert on
  `model_dump()` (the MCP union return nests under `structuredContent.result`).

4. File the survivors through `gh api` REST, labelled `enhancement`, `research` or `bug`.
5. Repeat until a round finds nothing new, or round 4, whichever comes first.

I'll also look through the codebase for a new batch of `good first issue` tickets. I'll post again when the research is back.

<result>I've saved the notes to `/Users/hosanglee/archy/research_notes/LLM code and software architecture/tools_landscape.md`, organised by your four questions. The most important finding is that SonarQube now does layer-style architecture rules for Python, free, and lets agents read them over MCP. Star counts below are from GitHub on 2026-10-26; every claim in the notes has a link, and vendor-only numbers are marked as such.

**Main findings**
- **SonarQube is now the closest competitor to `archy check`.** Its architecture management covers Python, Java, C#, JS and TS:
  - You define an allowed architecture (anything not allowed is forbidden), mark which parts of a component may be reached from outside, and violations become issues that block via quality gates.
  - Sonar can generate a first draft of the allowed architecture from the code as it is.
  - It is free on all SonarQube Cloud plans since 2026-03-19, and in SonarQube Server since 2026.4.
  - Its MCP server (v1.30, 2026-10-23) has architecture tools, including one that rewrites the allowed model with a dry run. Limits: views are capped at 150 nodes, editing the model is Cloud-only, and Python agents get only the read tools.
  - The Sonar sources conflict on cost: the feature is "on all plans", but the MCP README says the architecture tools need the Team or Enterprise plan on Cloud.
- **Two code-graph MCP servers now outnumber Aider on stars.** GitNexus has 48.0k stars and a noncommercial license; codebase-memory-mcp has 47.5k and is MIT. Between them they offer:
  - change impact from a git diff, with a risk rating
  - Cypher-style graph queries and a diff between two snapshots of the graph
  - hotspots and clusters
  - architecture decision records that agents can read and edit over MCP (codebase-memory-mcp)
  - installers that also add hooks and skills (codebase-memory-mcp covers 45 clients).

  None of them was found to ship layer rules with a pass/fail verdict, cycle gates, a DSM, co-change from git history, or trends over time. That is still archy's own ground.
- **CodeScene** now has an MCP server with Code Health tools for review, pre-commit and pre-push. Its pitch is "a deterministic gate the agent can't negotiate", and its accuracy figures are its own.
- **Moderne** has an MCP server built on OpenRewrite. Its own docs call it experimental and say agents don't call its tools consistently.
- **Tach** moved to `tach-org` and is maintained by the community since Gauge stopped working on it. Releases are maintenance-only, and some commands depend on a closed Gauge API that is expected to shut down.
- **import-linter** added no new contract type in 2026; its last two arrived in late 2025.
- **The other boundary linters** (dependency-cruiser, ArchUnit, deptrac, Packwerk) are active but have nothing for agents. Sheriff is the one exception: it added an AGENTS.md.
- **Two tools are cutting their MCP tool lists.** Nx now hides most of its tools by default in favour of skills, and Serena 2.0 replaced most of its tools with a single code-execution interface (and moved to GPL). That suggests a long tool list is now seen as a cost.
- **LLM code reviewers.** Only Sonar and CodeScene apply fixed, repeatable design checks. CodeRabbit, Greptile and Bugbot check architecture only through plain-English rule files given to an LLM, and Greptile's rules can't block a merge. Teams are starting to point all three at one shared REVIEW.md file.
- **Agent guardrails.** AGENTS.md has been a Linux Foundation standard since 2025-12-09 (60k+ adopting projects, OpenAI's figure). Claude Code's `PreToolUse` hook can block a tool call. Most tools in this space now have a one-command setup that writes AGENTS.md, MCP config, skills and hooks together.
- **Aider** hasn't been pushed to since 2026-05-22, so its repo map is a stale reference point.

**Ideas this suggests for archy**
- A rule that a package may only be imported through its public facade. Sonar, Tach and import-linter all ship this.
- Generating draft rules from the current import graph.
- Incremental adoption (leave some modules unchecked) and marking individual dependencies as deprecated, both from Tach.
- Architecture decision records linked to the archy rule that enforces each one. No tool found does this.
- Hook or skill installation alongside the MCP wiring. Given archy's six null results on pushing facts at the model, a blocking hook (enforcement) fits the evidence better than another way of injecting context.
- Writing archy findings into the REVIEW.md or AGENTS.md files that LLM reviewers already read.

**Not checked (listed as gaps in the notes):** Structure101/Sonargraph, Lattix, NDepend, jQAssistant, Sourcegraph/Amp, Qodo Merge, Graphite, Copilot code review, Cursor rules and hooks, and Sonar's AI Code Assurance details. I ran out of research budget before reaching these.</result>

<summary>Agent "Repo context research for agents" finished</summary>
<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>The notes are written. Overall, 2025 to 2026 evidence agrees with archy's six null results: pushing repository structure at frontier agents up front doesn't improve correctness. Where structural information does help, it helps agents find the right code, or it acts as a check after the edit.

File: `/Users/hosanglee/archy/research_notes/LLM code and software architecture/agent_context_evidence.md`

**1. Code graph systems.** Gains are real but small, and they come almost entirely from finding the right file or function, not from writing the patch.
- RepoGraph's headline "+32.8%" is a relative figure. In absolute terms it adds about 2 to 2.7 percentage points on SWE-bench Lite across four host systems.
- ARISE: +4.7 points, but it needed a data-flow graph down to individual statements.
- RepoAtlas: +2.4 points on SWE-bench Verified.
- Gains are largest when the issue text shares no words with the code that needs changing:
  - CodeCompass: +23.2 points on "hidden dependency" tasks, but only on one FastAPI repo.
  - KGCompass: 89.7% of the bugs it locates aren't named in the issue.
  - Bellam: each extra hop between the issue and the fix roughly halves small models' accuracy at finding the right function.
- Agents often don't call the tool at all:
  - In 58% of CodeCompass trials that had the graph, the agent never used it.
  - A language-server study found agents used the semantic tool 0 to 6% of the time when finding code, and the tool cost 6% to 118% more tokens.
  - Codebase-Memory used 10x fewer tokens but lost 9 points of answer quality (83% vs 92%).
- No paper tests import-level layer rules, cycles or dependency matrices. Every graph paper works at function, class or statement level, which the strongest results suggest is where any signal is.

**2. AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files.** The evidence is null to negative.
- ETH Zurich (Feb 2026): context files don't improve success rates, and LLM-generated ones raise cost by more than 20%.
  - Repository overviews didn't help any agent reach the relevant files faster, which is the closest published analogue to archy's briefs and headers.
  - Agents did follow the files' instructions, so the null isn't an adherence failure.
- Khatri (Jul 2026) ran Claude Code and Codex on 17 tasks. Context changed correctness by no more than 10 to 15 points either way. Agents failed on implementation skill, not on missing repository knowledge.
- A factorial study of 1,650 sessions found file size, position, structure and conflicting files had no effect on compliance. Compliance did fade by about 5.6% in odds with each function generated.
- The cost direction is contested: Lulla et al. found 16.6% fewer output tokens with an AGENTS.md, against ETH's +20%.
- Tool-surface studies find pass rates barely change between tool designs; what changes is cost and how consistent repeated runs are.

**3. Design and maintainability benchmarks.** Several 2026 benchmarks show that passing tests hides structural problems.
- SlopCodeBench: structure erodes in 77% of runs as agents extend their own code. Quality guidance given up front lowers the starting level by up to a third but doesn't slow the decay.
- SWE-CC: patches that pass tests still break 43.1% of the project's own contribution rules.
- SWE Refactor Bench: only 5.4% of runs fully pass. Agents fake migrations by copying the old code so tests pass.
- SWE-Maintain cuts the other way: agent-written code costs later tasks mainly through tests it left failing. Code that still passes earlier tests showed no measurable maintenance penalty.
- The most relevant positive is Code of Theseus. Recovered architecture documents didn't change pass rate (33.7% vs 35.8%), but the rebuilt module structure got significantly closer to the original (module F1 from 0.54 to 0.63). Structural context may move structure rather than pass rate or tokens, which are the axes archy measured.

**4. Feedback before vs after an edit.** No study compares the same information given before versus after an edit; that experiment is missing and could be archy's own pre-registered bench. Three signals point toward a check after the edit:
- SWE-agent's lint check on edits added 3 points (2024, background).
- A static-analysis feedback loop cut flagged issues from 40 to 80% down to 11 to 13%, though it was measured with the same tools that gave the feedback.
- Up-front guidance didn't change SlopCodeBench's decay rate, and instructions fade within a session.

**Caveats.** Many 2026 papers were read at abstract level only. I couldn't confirm ETH's "developer files beat LLM-generated ones by 7%" figure in the paper body. The Bellam numbers come from a summary of its code repository, not the paper. I didn't cover Moatless, AutoCodeRover's ablations or CodeRAG; they're listed as gaps in the notes.</result>

It runs about 4,100 words, contains no em dashes, and is built on all four research notes plus archy's own `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`, `bench/greenfield_results.md`, `docs/SPEC_INSTALL_HOOKS.md` and the open issues.

**The answer to the question:**
- **How agent code damages structure.** The strongest 2025-2026 evidence says it adds rather than integrates. It duplicates and re-implements existing functions, calls across files less, piles complexity into big functions, and produces oversized multi-file PRs (GitClear, MSR 2026 on real agent PRs, SlopCodeBench, the Cursor adoption study).
- **Layers and cycles.** Evidence that agents break layer rules or create import cycles is thin: one 15-run pilot and one study covering a single agent framework. That agrees with archy's own numbers (0 of 25 agent runs, 0.66% of commits).
- **Where the effect shows up.** Several careful studies found little or no quality effect (a preregistered RCT, a large real-repo measurement, SWE-Maintain). Damage appears mainly when supervision is low, volume is high, and agents keep extending their own code.
- **Review doesn't catch it.** Reviewers merge redundant agent code without objecting, and "architecture" is 0.3% of rejection reasons. PR size and spread is the structural property most consistently linked to rejection.
- **Before versus after the edit.** Outside studies now reproduce archy's six nulls. ETH found repository overviews in context files did not help any agent find the right file sooner. Instruction-following also decays within a session. Prompting for quality lowers where decay starts but not how fast it grows. Checks after the edit are the one placement with positive results, including archy's own 88% to 100% greenfield result.
- **Market.** SonarQube made its architecture enforcement free for Python on all Cloud plans in March 2026, with an MCP server. GitNexus and codebase-memory-mcp (about 48k stars each) give away blast radius, snapshot diff and hotspots. What archy still has that they don't is declared rules, co-change coupling from git history, and checking that nothing gets worse over time.

**Ranked features (the report gives evidence, the action it changes, and the null risk for each):**

| Rank | Feature | Risk of repeating the nulls |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | A check that fails only on new cycles or rule violations, `archy diff --strict` (#521) | Low |
| 2 | Opt-in after-edit hook that says nothing when the code is clean (spec already written) | Low to medium |
| 3 | Violation messages that name the allowed import route | Low to medium |
| 4 | Advisory finding when a PR re-implements an existing function, limited to functions the diff adds | Medium (precision) |
| 5 | Structural review summary on the PR from the GitHub Action | Low on the agent side, medium theater risk |
| 6 | Weekly drift check that opens an issue only when something new appears | Low |
| 7 | Draft rule file proposed from the current import graph, adoptable a module at a time | Medium |
| 8 | Overlap check for parallel agent branches | High |

The report also argues against more pre-edit context (the deferred brief in #427, ADR storage over MCP), new metrics with no action attached (a connectivity score, a per-module safety score), and more MCP tools.

It names one experiment no published study has run: the same rule given before the edit versus enforced after it, measured by how fast violations and duplication grow across iterations. It says that test only makes sense on agent-written code, where there is room for an effect, and only after piloting the control arm first.

A few sourcing caveats are stated in the report. GitClear's figures are correlational and come from a vendor. CodeScene's own pages give 30% in one place and 60% in another for the same defect-risk claim. The LinearB review-delay numbers were left out because the notes only had them second-hand.</result>

What external research cannot supply is the outcome archy most needs: no published study yet compares the *same* structural rule delivered before the edit against the same rule enforced after it, on the same tasks and model, measuring the slope of violations and duplication across iterations rather than pass rate. archy is unusually well placed to run that experiment honestly, but only in the regime with headroom (agent-written, iteratively extended code, where SlopCodeBench and the greenfield study found real rates), and only after piloting the control arm, since the last such study's win condition was arithmetically unreachable before it started.

The strategic implication is sharper than "add gates." Sonar now gives away intended-architecture enforcement for Python, and two free graph servers own the descriptive questions, so archy's credible position is the cheapest local ratchet on declared intent: free, offline, silent when the code is clean, specific about the fix when it is not. That position concedes that the event it guards is rare. The features worth building are the ones whose value survives that concession, because they cost nothing when nothing is wrong.

# Round 1 verdicts: report features #4 (diff-scoped duplicates) and #5 (PR review packet)

Reviewer stance: default REJECT. Repo state checked 2026-10-26 at `c5d9bcb` (v0.48.2). Read-only; nothing filed, no repo files edited.

---

## Candidate A: diff-scoped "re-implemented an existing function" finding

**VERDICT: FILE, but as a `research` ticket (pre-registered bench), not as a feature.** The feature ticket gets filed only if the bench passes.

### Gate 1: not a duplicate, not implemented. PASS

- `archy duplicates --help` (v0.48.2) has `--min-nodes`, `--top`, `--members`, `--co-change/--no-co-change`, `--near-miss`, `--format`. It has no `--since`, `--base` or diff scoping. `archy diff` compares against a snapshot baseline and has no duplicates content. `archy affected` maps files to tests.
- The duplicates arc is #133, #242, #246, #247 and #131 (all closed, completed). None of them scopes findings to added code. #521 (`diff --strict` ratchet) covers cycles and violations only. Nothing in the 202-issue dump matches "added function", "re-implement" or "AIDev".

### Gate 2: anti-theater. PASS, conditional on precision

The action is concrete: the author deletes the new copy and calls the existing function. It is not a number. That action only happens if most firings are real. At the measured precision for a fresh copy (see Gate 4) the reader chases one non-problem for every real one, which is what turned Study 9 (0.215) and Study 7 (0.024) into nulls.

### Gate 3: not on the closed delivery line. PASS

It fires after the edit, on the diff, only when a match exists, and it is advisory. It pushes nothing at the model before an edit. It would join the delivery line if someone wired it into a hook that prints every turn. The ticket rules that out.

### Gate 4: evidence says what the report claims. PARTIAL FAIL; this is why it is research first

- **Huang et al., arXiv 2601.21276** (notes `empirical_studies.md` l.16, l.62). The "nearly double" redundancy in agent PRs is an **embedding-based Type-4 (semantic) clone metric**, and the authors argue token/text clone detectors miss these clones. Our own notes say: "identical-cluster detection will miss" them. So the strongest piece of evidence is about clones that archy's AST-hash and token-multiset tiers **cannot see**. The report admits this ("will mostly be missed"), but it still uses this paper to motivate a detector that cannot measure what the paper measured. The report's own example (an agent writing a new `parse_date` beside `util/dates.parse_date`) is the Type-4 case: an independent re-implementation is unlikely to match an existing body's AST shape.
- **GitClear 2026**: correlational population trends, with no per-commit AI attribution, from a vendor that sells the measurement (notes l.15). "Cross-file calls down 35%" supports "less reuse". It is not evidence of within-repo function-level Type-1/2/3 copies.
- **SlopCodeBench 2.3x verbosity**: a custom composite metric over agents extending **their own** code (notes l.17, l.80). It says nothing about re-implementing a function that already existed in the repository.
- **Precision history** (`docs/LEARNINGS.md` l.295, `docs/SHIPPED.md` l.36/39, #242, #247): about 50% refactorability is the expected ceiling for similarity alone, and about 63% on the exact tier. The lift to about 74% comes from **co-change demotion** (`demote_independent`). That lever **abstains for a freshly added file**: `duplicates.py` l.487 skips any cluster with a file under `min_evidence` = 5 commits. A copy in a new file therefore falls back to the ~50-63% ceiling. Precision for this use case is unmeasured and likely lower than the shipped number.
- These precision numbers answer a different question anyway ("is this cluster refactorable?"). The feature asks something narrower: "should this new function have called the existing one?" No measurement exists for that.
- **Headroom is unknown.** How often an agent PR adds a body that matches an existing function at the exact or near-miss tier has never been counted. If the answer is near zero, the feature is the 0.66% problem again.

### Gate 5: scoped, with a test that goes red. PASS as a research ticket

The detector is a cheap filter over existing output, small enough for one PR. The work that actually decides the outcome is the measurement, so the ticket below is a pre-registered bench with a headroom kill and a precision kill.

### Ready ticket

**Title:** `research(duplicates): pre-register firing rate and precision of a diff-scoped "re-implemented an existing function" finding on agent PRs before building it`

**Labels:** `research`

**Body:**

> **Problem.** `archy duplicates` reports the duplication backlog for a whole repository. It cannot answer the question a reviewer has at change time: did this diff add a function that already exists elsewhere? Filtering clusters to those with one member in the diff's added lines and one member that already existed at the base commit would turn the report into a change-time check. We do not know if that check would fire often enough to matter, or if it would be right when it fires. archy has shipped two "obviously useful" detectors that missed their pre-registered precision bars: Study 7 (0.024 against 0.70) and Study 9 (0.215 against 0.40). Measure this one before building it.
>
> **Evidence.**
> - Agent PRs carry more redundancy than human PRs, but the measured kind is Type-4 (semantic, embedding-based), which AST and token-overlap detectors miss ([arXiv 2601.21276](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21276)). The finding is therefore expected to have low **recall** by design. This study measures firing rate and precision on the clones archy can see, and does not claim to cover the paper's effect.
> - GitClear 2026 reports falling cross-file reuse ([GitClear](https://www.gitclear.com/the_ai_code_quality_maintainability_gap)). The data is correlational and vendor-sourced.
> - Precision history: about 50% similarity-only ceiling, about 63% exact tier, about 74% source with co-change demotion (#242, #247, `docs/LEARNINGS.md`). The co-change lever abstains for files with fewer than 5 commits (`duplicates.py`, `min_evidence`), so a copy in a **new** file falls back toward the ceiling.
> - Dataset: AIDev ([HF hao-li/AIDev](https://huggingface.co/datasets/hao-li/AIDev)) ships `pull_request`, `pr_commit_details` (patches) and `pr_review_comments`, so the base commit, added hunks and reviewer reaction can be recovered per PR.
>
> **What changes for the user (the action), if it passes.** The PR author or the agent gets "new `f` in `a/x.py` matches existing `b/y.f`" and deletes the copy in favour of a call. If it fails, nobody builds it, and `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md` records why.
>
> **Scope.**
> 1. Write a pre-registration in `docs/research/DIFF_DUPLICATES_PRECISION.md` and commit it **before** the harness exists, with these thresholds:
>    - **Headroom kill:** fewer than 1 firing per 50 Python agent PRs in the main sample, or fewer than 30 scorable firings from at least 10 repositories. Either one means the feature is not built. This is a result, not "underpowered, try again".
>    - **Precision pass:** at least 0.60 over at least 30 scorable firings from at least 10 repositories, under the primary oracle.
>    - **Precision kill:** below 0.40.
>    - **Between 0.40 and 0.60:** null, and not shipped. No post-hoc subgroup rescues it. Subgroups (exact vs near-miss, new file vs existing file) are reported in full but are not results.
> 2. Pilot first, on a disjoint set of 20 PRs. The pilot measures firing rate and finds harness bugs only; no labels are read. Fix the thresholds after the pilot and before labeling, per AGENTS.md "pilot before you fix a threshold".
> 3. Harness `bench/diff_duplicates_precision.py`. For each Python AIDev PR (merged and closed), check out the base and head commits. Run the shipped detector (exact plus `near_miss` at the shipped 0.85 floor, `min_nodes` 30, source-only per #247) on head. Keep a cluster only if one member's `def` line falls inside an added hunk of base..head **and** another member existed at base outside the added hunks. Write one ledger row per PR in a single append, with only `status="ok"` counted as done. A crash in one PR does not end the run, and the run resumes from the ledger (copy `bench/_supervise.py` / `bench/q1b_run.py`).
> 4. `--canary` mode: a fixture PR that copies an existing function into a new file must fire, and a fixture PR that only edits an existing function must not. Run it before any real run, because both of Study 7's harness bugs produced publishable-looking numbers.
> 5. Oracles.
>    - **Primary:** blind labels from two labelers under a frozen rubric committed with the pre-registration. TRUE means "the new function should have called or reused the existing one". FALSE means "the duplication is intended or benign". Report agreement.
>    - **Secondary (reported, never decisive):** a git oracle that scores a firing TRUE if the copy was removed or consolidated in a later PR revision or within 6 months. It is biased against the feature, because reviewers do not object to redundant agent code (2601.21276).
>    - Firings that cannot be scored are dropped, never scored as clean.
>
> **Definition of done.**
> - The pre-registration is committed before the harness, and its commit hash is quoted in the results.
> - Unit tests for the added-hunk filter use a hand-built two-commit fixture. They go red when the "member existed at base" condition is removed, and red again when the "def line inside an added hunk" condition is removed. Clear `__pycache__` before each mutation. Assert that the fixture actually contains a pre-existing match before asserting the outcome.
> - The canary passes, the 20-PR pilot is reported, and the full run is complete.
> - Results go in `bench/diff_duplicates_precision_results.md` and a Study entry in `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`, published pass or fail.
> - If it passes, a separate feature ticket wires `--since <ref>` (or equivalent) to CLI text, CLI JSON and the `archy_duplicates` MCP payload, with a reason on every finding. That ticket is not this one.
>
> **Non-goals.**
> - No shipped CLI flag, MCP parameter or hook in this ticket.
> - Never a score input.
> - No embeddings or Type-4 detection. Embeddings would need their own measured precision gain.
> - No per-turn hook output. A hook that prints on every turn would be a seventh delivery-line intervention.
>
> From the 2026-10-26 research report.

---

## Candidate B: structural review packet posted by the GitHub Action

**VERDICT: REJECT as a new ticket. COMMENT on #327** (with #145 cross-referenced), recording the theater prune and the conditions for reopening.

### Gate 1: duplicate. FAIL

- **#145** "archy review: per-PR structural review brief for human judgment" (closed `not_planned` 2026-07-26 at the wind-down) already proposes the same packet content: blast radius, high-`edit_risk` touches, new cross-boundary edges phrased as reviewer questions, and an explicit "cannot vouch for" boundary.
- **#327** "feat(action): PR-comment surface" (closed `not_planned`, same day) is the delivery vehicle: an opt-in sticky comment on the composite action, safe on fork PRs, with blast radius, new cycles and violations. Its body says outright that #145 defines the content and #327 is where it lands.
- Candidate B is the union of the two, plus "co-change touches" and "split seams". Both tickets were parked because of the wind-down, not on merit, and archy is active again. The right move is a comment on the existing ticket, not a third ticket.
- Partly implemented already: `archy diff` builds a `DiffSummary` whose items (`cycle_added`, `violation_added`, `sdp_violation_added`, `required_reach_violation_added`, with resolved counterparts) each carry a `prompt` that rephrases the delta as the question a reviewer should answer (`diff.py` l.110-128, `diff_summary.py`). `action.yml` today runs only `score|check|cycles` and posts nothing.

### Gate 2: anti-theater, item by item

| Packet item | What the reviewer does differently | Keep? |
|---|---|---|
| New cycle / new forbidden-layer or contract crossing / new required-reach violation, with the import chain and the existing `DiffSummaryItem.prompt` | Asks for the edge to be removed or rerouted, or approves the rule exception explicitly | **KEEP.** This is #521's gate output rendered where review happens. >
> **Evidence.**
> - Agent PRs carry more redundancy than human PRs, but the measured kind is Type-4 (semantic, embedding-based), which AST and token-overlap detectors miss ([arXiv 2601.21276](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21276)). > - Precision history: about 50% similarity-only ceiling, about 63% exact tier, about 74% source with co-change demotion (#242, #247, `docs/LEARNINGS.md`). > **What changes for the user (the action), if it passes.** The PR author or the agent gets "new `f` in `a/x.py` matches existing `b/y.f`" and deletes the copy in favour of a call. If it fails, nobody builds it, and `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md` records why.
>
> **Scope.**
> 1. Write a pre-registration in `docs/research/DIFF_DUPLICATES_PRECISION.md` and commit it **before** the harness exists, with these thresholds:
>    - **Headroom kill:** fewer than 1 firing per 50 Python agent PRs in the main sample, or fewer than 30 scorable firings from at least 10 repositories. Either one means the feature is not built. This is a result, not "underpowered, try again".
>    - **Precision pass:** at least 0.60 over at least 30 scorable firings from at least 10 repositories, under the primary oracle.
>    - **Precision kill:** below 0.40.
>    - **Between 0.40 and 0.60:** null, and not shipped. No post-hoc subgroup rescues it. Subgroups (exact vs near-miss, new file vs existing file) are reported in full but are not results.
> 2. Pilot first, on a disjoint set of 20 PRs. The pilot measures firing rate and finds harness bugs only; no labels are read. Fix the thresholds after the pilot and before labeling, per AGENTS.md "pilot before you fix a threshold".
> 3. Harness `bench/diff_duplicates_precision.py`. For each Python AIDev PR (merged and closed), check out the base and head commits. Run the shipped detector (exact plus `near_miss` at the shipped 0.85 floor, `min_nodes` 30, source-only per #247) on head. Keep a cluster only if one member's `def` line falls inside an added hunk of base..head **and** another member existed at base outside the added hunks. Write one ledger row per PR in a single append, with only `status="ok"` counted as done. A crash in one PR does not end the run, and the run resumes from the ledger (copy `bench/_supervise.py` / `bench/q1b_run.py`).
> 4. `--canary` mode: a fixture PR that copies an existing function into a new file must fire, and a fixture PR that only edits an existing function must not. Run it before any real run, because both of Study 7's harness bugs produced publishable-looking numbers.
> 5. Oracles.
>    - **Primary:** blind labels from two labelers under a frozen rubric committed with the pre-registration. TRUE means "the new function should have called or reused the existing one". FALSE means "the duplication is intended or benign". Report agreement.
>    - **Secondary (reported, never decisive):** a git oracle that scores a firing TRUE if the copy was removed or consolidated in a later PR revision or within 6 months. It is biased against the feature, because reviewers do not object to redundant agent code (2601.21276).
>    - Firings that cannot be scored are dropped, never scored as clean.
>
> **Definition of done.**
> - The pre-registration is committed before the harness, and its commit hash is quoted in the results.
> - Unit tests for the added-hunk filter use a hand-built two-commit fixture. They go red when the "member existed at base" condition is removed, and red again when the "def line inside an added hunk" condition is removed. Clear `__pycache__` before each mutation. Assert that the fixture actually contains a pre-existing match before asserting the outcome.
> - The canary passes, the 20-PR pilot is reported, and the full run is complete.

> - Never a score input.
> - No embeddings or Type-4 detection. Embeddings would need their own measured precision gain.
> - No per-turn hook output. A hook that prints on every turn would be a seventh delivery-line intervention.

### VERDICT: COMMENT on #132 (and reopen it once #521 has merged)

Comment text:

> Reopening proposal from the 2026-10-26 research report (archy is active again; this was closed only in the 2026-07-26 bulk park).
>
> The design should change in three ways before anyone builds it.
>
> **1. Gate on the #521 ratchet, not `score --strict`.** A new 2-module cycle in a 600-module repo moves the tangle ratio by about 0.003, inside the 0.02 tolerance (#521), so `score --strict` misses exactly what this hook exists to catch. The hook runs `archy diff --strict` and blocks only on a new cycle or a new violation. Blocked on #521.
>
> **2. Silent on pass, always.** The spec's "advisory by default: run the gate, surface the result" would print on every turn, which is a seventh push channel; Study 8 measured two such pushes as 1.26x and 1.128x more expensive (`docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`). On pass the wrapper writes nothing to stdout or stderr and exits 0. On a new finding it blocks (Claude Code: exit 2, reason on stderr) and names the offending modules and edge, nothing else. A crash or a missing baseline never blocks and never masquerades as a finding (the local `archy_gate.sh` already learned this from a `FileNotFoundError` that trapped the agent).
>
> **3. Claude Code only for the first PR.** Cursor, Codex and opencode each need a bespoke adapter (the spec documents different event models), and the 2026-10 research did not re-verify Cursor's hook contract. Add other clients only after a usage signal (#536) shows anyone installs the first one.
>
> **Scope of the first PR.** A hidden `archy hook gate` command that owns the exit-code contract; `hook_actions` on the Claude Code adapter (`Stop` only, never `PostToolUse`, which fires 5 to 15 times per task per `docs/FUTURE.md`); `archy install --hooks` and `archy uninstall --hooks` as exact inverses via the existing render/unrender pairs; default `--location local`.
>
> **Definition of done.**
> - A test where the baseline is clean and the tree gains a forbidden import: `archy hook gate` exits 2 and stderr names the source, target and rule. Mutation-verified: make the wrapper return 0 unconditionally, clear `__pycache__`, confirm red.
> - A test where nothing new appears (including a baseline that already carries a violation): exit 0 and **empty** stdout and stderr, asserted byte-for-byte. Mutation-verified by making the pass path print a summary.
> - A test where archy itself raises: exit 0, non-blocking note, never exit 2.
> - Install then uninstall leaves the client settings file byte-identical (idempotency, same harness as the installer tests).
>
> **What not to claim.** On existing code the hook will rarely fire: 0 of 25 agent runs (#356) and 0.66% of commits (#359) introduced a new finding. The measured regime with headroom is scaffolding (3 of 25 unaided greenfield runs had the dependency direction wrong, #369). No study yet shows a hook beats a prompted pull of the same checker; do not state a benefit in the README.
>
> From the 2026-10-26 research report.

### Comment text for #521

> Note from the 2026-10-26 research report (feature #6, "scheduled drift sensor"), reviewed and not filed as its own ticket.
>
> A scheduled drift sensor reduces to this ticket: `archy diff --strict` against the committed baseline, run from the user's own `on: schedule:` trigger around the planned Action `command: diff`. It is not usable before this lands, because plain `diff` keys cycles by `frozenset(modules)` and a weekly job would report every SCC membership change as a new cycle. So no separate ticket.
>
> One small request that serves both the per-PR and any scheduled use: when `--strict` fails, print each offending edge as `path:line` (source file and import line) in the text reason, the JSON, and the MCP `DiffReport`. `Violation.lines` and `CycleEdge.lines` already carry the line, so this needs no new data, and it makes "which commit introduced this" a single `git blame -L <line>,<line> -- <path>` for anyone who wants it. archy itself should not run blame or open issues; `docs/SPEC_INSTALL_TESTING.md` already records why unwatched cron alerting turns into noise.
>
> If this is folded in, the acceptance list gains one case: the reason for a new forbid violation contains the source path and the import's line number, asserted on `model_dump()` and on the text output, and verified red by dropping the line from the renderer.
>
> Revisit a documented scheduled recipe only if an adopter asks for it (see #536 for how adopters are counted).

---


XXXXX
### Comment text for #535

```
Two more facts for part 1 and part 2, found by the 2026-10-26 research report and checked against the sources today.

**SonarQube fires falsifier 1 harder than optave does.** Architecture management (current graph, an intended allow-list architecture, "interfaces" for which children are reachable from outside, deviations raised as quality-gate issues) became available on all SonarQube Cloud plans, including Free/OSS, on 2026-03-19, with Python supported, and in all commercial SonarQube Server editions from 2026.4.
- https://community.sonarsource.com/t/architecture-is-now-available-for-everyone-on-sonarqube-cloud/179844
- https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-cloud/architecture

So `CODEGRAPH_COMPETITIVE_ANALYSIS.md:272` ("every graph tool in its category ... has no representation of the structure you intended") is false for the best-known vendor in the space, not only for a 99-star project.

What still holds against Sonar, to keep the narrowed sentence honest:
- Not local or offline: Cloud needs an account and server-side analysis; Server is commercial editions only.
- Agent access is paid: the sonarqube-mcp-server README says the `architecture` toolset "requires a Team or Enterprise plan" on Cloud, intended-architecture reads are Cloud-only, and current views are capped at 150 nodes (https://github.com/SonarSource/sonarqube-mcp-server). Do not write "free with MCP".
- I did not find transitive contracts, a cycle ratchet or a trended score in the Sonar docs; check before claiming any of them as unique.

**Descriptive substitutes for impact/diff/hotspots.** GitNexus (48,049 stars, https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus; PolyForm Noncommercial per its repo, so free only for noncommercial use) and codebase-memory-mcp (47,540 stars, MIT, https://github.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp) ship git-diff blast radius, impact analysis and, for codebase-memory-mcp, snapshot comparison (`compare_graphs`) and hotspots, per their READMEs. When part 2 narrows §6, check snapshot/diff and hotspots against codebase-memory-mcp as well as optave's `snapshot.ts` / `branch-compare.ts` before listing either as a difference.

Part 4 (`docs/LEARNINGS.md:245`, "all of {Python-native, import-graph, layer rules, trended score, MCP server}") probably still survives Sonar, since Sonar is multi-language rather than Python-native; worth one line confirming it.

From the 2026-10-26 research report.
```

content.text:
Round 1 of the loop has finished and its results are posted on GitHub. Round 2 is running now: a new agent is looking through the research notes for ideas the report didn't cover and testing each one against the same gates. The good-first-issue search is still running too.

Round 1 put eight candidates through the gates. One became a new ticket, four became comments on existing tickets, and the other four were rejected.

**New ticket:** #548 (`research`). Run a pre-registered measurement on agent PRs (the AIDev dataset) before building a check that flags a function a PR re-implements. The check is only built if precision reaches 0.60 or more, and it is dropped below 0.40 or if it fires less than once per 50 PRs. It is a measurement first because the strongest study found semantic duplicates (same logic, different code) that archy's duplicate detector cannot see.

**Comments on existing tickets:**
- **#132, after-edit hook:** run the #521 check instead of `score --strict`, print nothing when the code is clean, and support only Claude Code at first. I did not reopen it; the comment says to wait until #521 merges.
- **#521, `archy diff --strict`:** a scheduled drift check is just this command on a cron. The one addition is to print `path:line` for each offending import, so `git blame` finds the commit that introduced it.
- **#535, positioning:** SonarQube made its architecture rules free for Python on 2026-03-19. Its agent (MCP) access to them needs a paid plan, so "free with MCP" would be wrong. GitNexus and codebase-memory-mcp now give away blast-radius and snapshot-diff features.
- **#327, PR review comment:** I cut the proposed packet down to the items a reviewer would actually act on. It stays closed until #521 ships and at least one outside repo is shown to run the Action.

**Rejected:**
- **Violation messages naming the allowed import route:** `archy.yaml` only lists what is forbidden. On a test fixture the suggested route was one `archy contracts` flags as broken.
- **Draft rule file from the current imports:** it would pass on day one by construction, and #122 and #288 already closed this idea.
- **Before-vs-after experiment:** archy already ran it as #369 (88% vs 100%, with too little room to show a difference).
- **Parallel-agent overlap check:** no measured conflict rate exists anywhere.

The full report is at `/Users/hosanglee/archy/reports/LLM code and software architecture.md`, with the research notes beside it under `research_notes/`. Neither folder is committed.

Ranked by confidence:

1. **fix(mcp):** `archy_score` takes any `strict_tolerance`. The CLI rejects values outside [0, 1], but over MCP a value of 5.0 makes the regression gate pass. The same score drop shows `passed=False` at 0.02 and `passed=True` at 5.0.
2. **test(cli):** I disabled each of the 21 CLI bound checks one at a time and ran the full suite. Five changes left the suite green: `duplicates --top` and `--members`, `render --focus-depth` and `--max-nodes`, and `brief --top`. With the `--members` check gone the user gets a traceback, and the existing test still passes because it only checks `exit_code != 0`.
3. **test:** 17 tests fail for a contributor whose global git config signs commits (15 failures plus 2 errors). One autouse fixture in a new `tests/conftest.py` that isolates the git config fixes it; I confirmed this by loading that fixture as a plugin.
4. **fix(mcp):** a path that doesn't exist is created on disk (`<path>/.archy/index.db`, and `baseline.json` from `archy_snapshot`). That empty project then gets a perfect 1.0 score. The CLI rejects the same path. This is narrower than #523, which is about real directories that contain 0 modules.
5. **fix(dsm):** `archy dsm --diff` on a file that isn't a DSM snapshot crashes with a traceback (`JSONDecodeError`, `KeyError: 'ordering'`), for example when given `archy graph --format json` output.
6. **fix(diff):** `archy diff --baseline` on malformed JSON or `{}` crashes with a traceback.
7. **fix(mcp):** `archy_cycles(min_size=0 or -5)` and `archy_dsm(focus_depth=-1)` are accepted, although the CLI rejects both. #170 fixed only the CLI side.
8. **fix(dsm):** `--focus` with a module name that doesn't exist prints an empty matrix and exits 0. Combined with `--diff`, it reports every module as removed.
9. **fix(cli):** `graph` and `cycles` are the only commands that require PATH; the other 17 default to `.`.
10. **docs(tour):** `docs/SIXTY_SECOND_TOUR.md` says the score averages four axes, shows sample output without the complexity line, and gives an old `mcp` version pin.
11. **docs(contributing):** `CONTRIBUTING.md:125` says to use frozen dataclasses for value objects. The code has none; it uses about 100 frozen pydantic models instead.

Against the issue list, I opened the closest matches (#162, #163, #167, #170, #171, #523, #524) and none duplicates a candidate. The file also lists what I dropped and why: the `affected -j/--json` flag inconsistency (changing it needs a deprecation decision), the duplicated `_git` test helpers (better filed after #3 lands), and two leads that turned out not to be bugs.

`git status` shows no changes to tracked files. Two untracked directories are present: `research_notes/` was there at the start, and `reports/` (containing "LLM code and software architecture.md", timestamped 10:32) appeared during the session but wasn't created by me, so I left it alone.</result>

## 6. A global install writes an always-on pre-edit instruction block into every project

**VERDICT: FILE**

Refutation attempts, gate by gate:

- **Gate 1:** not a duplicate. #534 rewrites skill and loop-prompt wording and explicitly says "Leave `src/archy/install/base.py` alone". #132 is hooks. #427 is a deferred brief. A search for "global CLAUDE.md", "rules file", "instructions block" and "location global" finds nothing on placement. Verified as current behaviour: with a fake `HOME`, `archy install --print-config claude` writes the block to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and `--print-config codex` writes it to `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`. `--location` defaults to `global` (`cli.py:1615-1617`).
- **Gate 2:** a different action follows. In a non-Python repository, following the block's "Take a baseline with `archy_snapshot` at the start of a task" writes `.archy/baseline.json` and reports `score: 1.000 cycles: 0 violations: 0`, exit 0. I reproduced this on a scratch TypeScript repo (`round2/jsrepo`). After the change, agents in projects the user never pointed archy at stop making that call and stop seeing a perfect score for a language archy cannot parse. This removes an action rather than adding a number.
- **Gate 3:** it moves away from the closed delivery line, because it withdraws a push.
- **Gate 4:** the evidence supports withdrawing the push, not claiming a saving. ETH: context-file instructions "are well followed by coding agents" but do not improve success and raise cost by over 20%, for both LLM-generated and developer-written files (abstract checked). Study 8: two pushes through archy's own channel cost 1.26x and 1.128x. Neither study measured this block, so the ticket claims no saving. Strongest counter-argument: without the block, agents in Python repos may call archy less (CodeCompass: 58% of trials with graph access made zero calls). Answer: no archy measurement shows those calls help (median zero calls before the first edit, six pushes with none positive), and a project install keeps the block where the user opted in.
- **Gate 5:** one PR across the install adapters, `base.py`, docs and syrupy snapshots, with a migration path and a test that goes red. MCP and CLI analysis output are untouched, so the three-surface rule does not apply. The install surfaces are `install`, `uninstall` and `--print-config`.

**Body:**

**Problem.** `archy install` defaults to `--location global` (`src/archy/cli.py:1615-1617`). On that path every adapter writes the marker-fenced block from `src/archy/install/base.py:79` into a client-wide instruction file: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (adapters/claude.py:74), `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` (adapters/codex.py:47), `~/.cursor/rules/archy.mdc`, the opencode `AGENTS.md`, and `~/.continue/rules/archy.md`. Claude Code and Codex load their global file in every session of every project. The block (about 1,350 characters) tells the agent to "Ask it before you decide", to call `archy_impact` "Before editing", and to "Take a baseline with `archy_snapshot` at the start of a task".

So a user who installs archy for one Python project now has that instruction in their TypeScript, Go and documentation repositories too. Following it there is not harmless. On a scratch repo containing only `src/index.ts`, `archy snapshot` writes `.archy/baseline.json` and prints `score: 1.000  cycles: 0  violations: 0` with exit 0. The agent gets a perfect score for code archy cannot read, plus an untracked file in the user's tree (related: #523).

**Evidence.**
- Instructions in context files are followed, but they do not improve task success and raise inference cost by over 20%, for LLM-generated and developer-written files alike: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988
- Thoughtworks Radar Vol. 34 puts "agent instruction bloat" on Caution: https://www.thoughtworks.com/radar/techniques
- archy's own delivery line: six interventions, none positive, the last two costing 1.26x and 1.128x their controls (`docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`, Study 8).
- Nx's MCP server now defaults to `--minimal` and moves guidance into on-demand skills: https://nx.dev/docs/reference/nx-mcp

None of these measured this block, so this ticket claims no token or cost saving.

**What changes for the user.** `archy install` with the default global location registers the MCP server and seeds the Claude permission allowlist, and writes no instruction block. Running `archy install --location local` inside a Python project still writes the block into that project's `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` / rules file, so the guidance appears only where the user opted archy in. Re-running a global install on a machine that already has the global block removes it.

**Scope.**
- In each adapter's `plan()`, emit the `kind="instructions"` `FileAction` only when `scope == "local"`.
- For a global install, add an action that strips an existing archy block using the existing `remove_instructions` / `delete_file` unrender paths. The user's own text around the markers must stay byte-identical. For files archy owns outright (`rules/archy.mdc`, `rules/archy.md`), delete the file.
- `--print-config <id>` for global shows no instruction file, or shows the removal.
- Update `docs/INSTALL.md` ("What gets installed", item 2, and the path matrix) and README.md:470.
- Regenerate the syrupy snapshots in `tests/install/snapshot`.

**Definition of done.**
- On a fake `HOME`, a test runs a global install for every adapter. `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` are not created when absent, and a pre-existing one with user text is byte-identical afterwards. Mutation-verified: restore the unconditional instructions `FileAction`, clear `__pycache__`, confirm red.
- A migration test: a global file holding user text plus an old archy block comes out as just the user text, byte-identical, after a global install.
- A guard test: a local install still writes the block into the project file, so the fix cannot pass by deleting the block everywhere. Mutation-verified by dropping the local branch.
- Install, then uninstall, still leaves every client file byte-identical (the existing idempotency harness).
- The full CI set is green: `uv run ruff check` (no path), `ruff format --check`, `ty check`, `pytest`, `archy check .`, `archy cycles . --strict`, `archy conventions . --emit-headers --check`.

**Non-goals.**
- No claim that removing the block saves tokens or improves agents. Nothing measured it.
- Not rewording the local block (that wording belongs with #534).
- Not changing MCP tool descriptions or the `loop` prompt.
- No hooks (#132).
- Not making `snapshot` refuse non-Python trees (#523 covers the 0-module clean pass).

From the 2026-10-26 research report.

## 7. The installed block's pre-edit wording

**VERDICT: COMMENT on #534**

- **Gate 1:** this extends #534, whose own premise for excluding `base.py` is factually wrong.
- **Gate 2:** same as #534: the guidance stops asserting an unmeasured pre-edit cadence.
- **Gate 3:** it withdraws a push.
- **Gate 4:** the text is quoted directly from the file.
- **Gate 5:** it fits inside #534's PR, at the cost of one snapshot regeneration.

**Comment text:**

> One correction to the scope. The ticket says to leave `src/archy/install/base.py` alone because its rules text "already says 'after edits, call archy_diff', not a per-edit cadence". The same block also says, at `base.py:82` "Ask it before you decide, not only after you edit", at `base.py:87` "Before editing, call `archy_impact` ...", and at `base.py:99` "Take a baseline with `archy_snapshot` at the start of a task". These are the same unmeasured pre-edit cadence this ticket removes from the skill and the loop prompt, in the one surface that `archy install` writes into users' own instruction files. The `archy_snapshot` tool description (`mcp.py:932-941`) makes the same claim: "Read it up front to avoid proposing a cross-layer or cycle-introducing edit, rather than being told after the diff."
>
> Suggest folding both into this PR:
> - In `INSTRUCTIONS_BODY`, drop the "before you decide" lead and the "Before editing" bullet. Keep the lookup bullets (`archy_check(contracts=True)` for reachability, `archy_module_view` for "does X import Y") as pull answers to a named question, and frame `archy_diff` / `archy_check` as the verification step before commit.
> - In the `archy_snapshot` description, drop the "Read it up front to avoid proposing..." sentence.
> - Regenerate the syrupy snapshots in `tests/install/snapshot`. That is a one-command cost, not a reason to keep the text.
> - Extend the acceptance grep to `src/archy/install/` and `src/archy/mcp.py` for "before you decide", "Before editing" and "up front to avoid".
>
> Same anti-theater framing as the ticket: this stops asserting a benefit, and it does not claim a behaviour change. Separately, where the block is written at all (every global install puts it in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`, so it reaches non-Python projects) is a placement question, filed on its own.
>
> From the 2026-10-26 research report.

## 8. The ratchet's baseline can be rewritten by the tool the agent is told to call first

**VERDICT: COMMENT on #521**

- **Gate 1:** this is a design constraint on #521 and on the #132 hook comment, not a new feature.
- **Gate 2:** a different action follows. A new cycle stays blocked even after an agent follows its standing instruction to re-baseline.
- **Gate 3:** it acts after the edit.
- **Gate 4:** the code facts are verified. `archy_diff(path)` (`mcp.py:960`) takes no baseline argument and reads `PATH/.archy/baseline.json`. `archy_snapshot` overwrites that same file and is annotated `readOnlyHint=True` (`mcp.py:931`). The docstring at `mcp.py:703-711` justifies that because the file is "a cache/baseline the next call reads, not an external side effect", which stops being true once the file is a gate input. The installed block (`base.py:99`) and the `loop` prompt both tell agents to snapshot at the start of a task. Deliberate tampering is NOT evidenced: across 25 greenfield arm-B transcripts there were 25 tool calls touching `archy.yaml`, all reads and no writes (the prompt forbade edits). The risk is the instructed workflow, not adversarial agents.
- **Gate 5:** one test, plus the annotation change, inside #521's PR.

**Comment text:**

> A design constraint worth pinning before this is built: the baseline the ratchet compares against must be one that `archy_snapshot` cannot overwrite.
>
> Today `archy_diff(path)` over MCP (`src/archy/mcp.py:960`) takes no baseline argument, so it always reads `PATH/.archy/baseline.json`. `archy_snapshot` writes that same file. It is annotated `readOnlyHint=True, idempotentHint=True` (`mcp.py:931`), on the stated grounds that the file is "a cache/baseline the next call reads, not an external side effect" (`mcp.py:703-711`), so clients that auto-approve read-only tools will let it run without asking. The installed instructions (`install/base.py:99`) and the `loop` prompt both tell agents to snapshot at the start of a task. Once `.archy/baseline.json` is the strict gate's reference, an agent that hits a failing `diff --strict` and then starts its next task as instructed grandfathers its own new cycle, and every surface reports a pass. No tampering is needed. (For calibration: in the 25 greenfield arm-B transcripts, the 25 tool calls touching `archy.yaml` were all reads, so this is not a claim that agents game configs.)
>
> Suggested additions to scope:
> - `--strict` on every surface reads only the committed `--baseline <path>` file this ticket already proposes, and fails with a stated reason if that file is absent. It never silently falls back to `.archy/baseline.json`. On MCP this means `archy_diff` grows an optional `baseline` argument, or a strict mode that resolves the committed file.
> - `archy_snapshot` never writes the committed baseline path. It keeps writing `.archy/baseline.json` for the per-task, non-strict diff.
> - Correct the annotation for `archy_snapshot` (and `archy_score` when `record=True`) to `readOnlyHint=False`, `destructiveHint=True`, and update the `mcp.py:703-711` rationale.
> - The text, JSON and `DiffReport` outputs name the baseline path the verdict used.
>
> Acceptance case: commit a baseline, add a 2-cycle, call MCP `archy_snapshot`, then run strict diff against the committed baseline. It must still fail and name the cycle. Mutation-verified by pointing strict mode at `.archy/baseline.json`, which should turn the test red. The #132 hook proposal should then call the strict command with the committed baseline, never the default path.
>
> From the 2026-10-26 research report.

content.text:
Round 3 of the loop is running.

Round 2 produced one new ticket and two comments:
- **#560** (`enhancement`): a global `archy install` writes archy's "call it before you edit" block into the agent's global instruction file (for Claude Code, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`), so agents see it in every project. Following it in a repo with no Python reports a perfect 1.000 score. The fix writes the block only on `--location local`.
- **Comment on #534:** `install/base.py` makes the same unmeasured "call it before editing" claims the ticket removes elsewhere, so it should be in scope.
- **Comment on #521:** the ratchet must read a committed baseline. `archy_snapshot` overwrites `.archy/baseline.json`, and the instructions tell agents to snapshot at the start of every task, so an agent following them would wipe its own new cycle from the comparison.

The 11 new `good first issue` tickets, #549 to #559, were reproduced on main, and I re-checked one of them, #549, myself. All 11 are labelled `good first issue` plus `bug`, `enhancement` or `documentation`.
- 549: `archy_score` over MCP accepts a `strict_tolerance` of 5.0 and passes every regression.
- 550: five CLI bound checks can be deleted with the test suite staying green.
- 551: 17 tests fail for anyone whose git config signs commits.
- 552: over MCP, a path that doesn't exist gets created on disk and scored a perfect 1.0.
- 553: `archy dsm --diff` crashes with a traceback when given a file that isn't a DSM snapshot.
- 554: `archy diff --baseline` crashes on malformed JSON.
- 555: the MCP `archy_cycles` and `archy_dsm` tools accept `min_size` and `focus_depth` values the CLI rejects.
- 556: `archy dsm --focus` with a name that matches no module exits 0 with an empty matrix.
- 557: `graph` and `cycles` are the only commands that require a PATH.
- 558: the 60-second tour describes four score axes and leaves out the complexity line.
- 559: `CONTRIBUTING.md` says to use frozen dataclasses, but the code uses frozen pydantic models.

**Most important finding, for #535: hello2morrow's Zügel MCP server.** It overlaps archy more than any tool covered so far, including Sonar, because it runs locally and supports Python:
- It is commercial and free with a Sonargraph-Architect license. Python support arrived in 26.4.1, and the current version is 26.6.1 (released 2026-09-30).
- It ships architecture rules written in a DSL, a list of violations, and module and package cycles.
- It keeps baselines and treats violations and cycles as a ratchet that may only go down.
- It answers dependency queries, suggests where to cut a cycle, keeps a "prevention" ledger, and has a tool the agent calls to check a new dependency before writing it.
- It explicitly markets checking before the edit, which is the placement archy measured as null six times.

This is a new reason to retire the "only tool" claims in #535.

| # | Candidate (source) | Verdict | Main reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `archy cycles` suggests which edges to cut, or a module to move (Zügel, Sonargraph, Lattix) | REJECT | Listing, locating and pricing cuts already exist (`cycles`, `dsm --group=topological`, `simulate --remove`). Zügel's own docs say the cheapest cut can point the wrong way unless rules are declared, and where layers are declared `archy check` already names the upward edge. Study 4 found nobody paying down standing violations. |
| 2 | Named or per-branch baselines (Zügel, Lattix) | REJECT | Named baselines already exist (`snapshot --out`, `diff --baseline`). A baseline built from the base branch would replace #521's committed-baseline design, which you said not to re-propose. My fixture shows `archy diff` can't say which edge closed a new cycle, but #521 already covers naming the closing edge(s). |
| 3 | Prevention ledger or per-rule acceptance stats (Zügel, Graphite) | REJECT | It is a number for display that changes nobody's action, and it records pre-edit calls (the closed delivery line). |
| 4 | Duplication gate on new code only (Sonar's "Sonar way for agentic AI" gate fails a PR above 3% duplication on new code) | **COMMENT on #548** | Checked on Sonar's own docs. Sonar needs at least 100 tokens over 10 lines and does not ignore renamed identifiers. The comment asks #548 to report, without changing its thresholds, what share of true hits Sonar's gate would also have failed.
